Grain growth is a classic materials kinetics process driven by the tendency of a polycrystalline material to reduce its total grain-boundary energy. A grain boundary has an interfacial energy gamma (J/m^2), so the total grain-boundary energy can be written approximately as G_gb = gamma * A_gb, where A_gb is the total grain-boundary area. Because the system tries to lower its free energy, it tends to reduce total grain-boundary area. This is why small grains tend to disappear and larger grains tend to grow during annealing (as you have seen it with the MC simulation).
The local driving force for grain-boundary motion comes from boundary curvature. A curved boundary has a pressure-like thermodynamic driving force proportional to gamma * kappa, where kappa is the local curvature. The kinetic response of the boundary is written as v_n = M * P, or for curvature-driven growth, v_n = M * gamma * kappa. Here v_n is the normal grain-boundary velocity, M is the grain-boundary mobility, gamma is the grain-boundary energy, and kappa is the curvature. This means that the boundary velocity increases when the mobility is high, when the grain-boundary energy is high, or when the curvature is large.
The mobility is treated as a thermally activated quantity using an Arrhenius equation: M(T) = M0 * exp(-Qm / (R * T)). In this expression, M0 is the pre-exponential factor, Qm is the activation energy for grain-boundary motion, R is the gas constant, and T is the absolute temperature. The pre-exponential factor M0 sets the overall scale of the mobility, while the exponential term exp(-Qm / (R * T)) gives the strong temperature dependence. At low temperature, the exponential term is very small, so mobility is low and grain growth is slow. At high temperature, the exponential term becomes much larger, so mobility rises rapidly and grain growth becomes much faster.
In this simulation, the physical grain-growth law will be based on the 2D von Neumann-Mullins relation. For an ideal 2D polycrystalline structure with isotropic grain-boundary energy and isotropic mobility, the rate of area change of an n-sided grain is given by dA/dt = K * (n - 6), where K = (pi / 3) * gamma * M. This is a very important result in grain-growth theory because it says that, in 2D, the area change rate depends only on the number of sides of the grain (this is of course an approximation). If n > 6, then dA/dt > 0 and the grain grows. If n < 6, then dA/dt < 0 and the grain shrinks. If n = 6, then dA/dt = 0 (meta stable), meaning the grain is neutral in area under ideal conditions.
The factor K = (pi / 3) * gamma * M is the kinetic prefactor used in the simulation. It combines the thermodynamic term gamma and the kinetic term M into a single effective growth-rate coefficient. Since M itself follows an Arrhenius equation, K also becomes strongly temperature dependent. This means that the simulation naturally predicts faster grain growth at higher temperature and slower grain growth at lower temperature.
The simulation does not explicitly solve the local curvature field of every grain boundary. Instead, it uses the von Neumann-Mullins result as the target physical law. Over one timestep dt, the target area change for each grain is calculated as deltaA = K * (n - 6) * dt. This gives the physically expected increase or decrease in grain area during that timestep. In other words, the simulation first decides how much a grain should grow or shrink according to materials kinetics, and only then applies a numerical method to produce that change geometrically.
The numerical geometry in this model will be based on a power-Voronoi construction (it is an interesting mathematical model to generate some cells with relation to each other. It is very usefull for grain growth simulations). Each grain is represented by a seed point and a weight (Vorono paramters). Changing the weight changes the size of the corresponding Voronoi cell. Therefore, the simulation needs a way to convert the physically required area change deltaA into a numerical weight change deltaw. To do that, it estimates the sensitivity dA/dw numerically using a small perturbation eps_w (that parameter should be a constant, do not play with it). The derivative is approximated as dA/dw ≈ (A(w + eps_w) - A(w)) / eps_w. This will tell the code how much the grain area changes when the grain weight is changed slightly.
Using this sensitivity, the code builds a global calibration factor C so that the numerical update can be written approximately as deltaw = C * deltaA. Therefore, the physical equations determine how much the area should change, while the power-Voronoi weights are the numerical mechanism used to realize that area change in the simulated microstructure. That C parameter is also for converting Voronoi-scale into our area scale. It is nothing related to kinetics.
The parameter eps for dA/dw is not a physical materials parameter. It is only a numerical parameter used to estimate the derivative dA/dw.
